newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam wary about racking up foreign debts.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam wary about racking up foreign debts.

text.p: Vietnam is concentrating its efforts on mobilising domestic savings rather than borrowing from abroad, a senior central bank official said.

In an interview broadcast on Reuters Financial Television on Wednesday, Tran Trong Do, the State Bank of Vietnam's banking operations director said: "We think that domestic savings are more important than...foreign capital inflows."
"If we borrow a lot from foreign countries that will be a debt burden for future generations. That's why we try to mobilise domestic savings," he said.
Do said there was a significant amount of money in circulation and the public needed to be encouraged to deposit in in the banking system.

Analysts say the bank's recent decision to allow the dong to depreciate against the dollar was aimed at narrowing the country's yawning trade gap and at flushing out dollars which millions of people have saved at home.
Seven weeks ago the bank widened the permitted interbank trading band for the dong to plus or minus five percent around a daily indicative rate from plus or minus one percent.
Since then, the dong has dropped four percent to its new floor of 11,653 per dollar.

Do said inflation in Vietnam was higher than in the United States at a time when the authorities kept the dong at a rate of around 11,000 per dollar. That meant there had been a real appreciation of the dong, he said.
"It was necessary to make a minor adjustment," he said.
However, he said the central bank's most important job was to stabilise the currency and implement the new policy on a gradual basis to avoid sending shockwaves through the economy.
Vietnam has increasingly expressed concern about borrowing from abroad and, in particular, short-term debt to finance imports.

The country had hoped to make a debut international bond issue last year, but on advice from the World Bank, had decided to hold off until finalising a reschedule of its roughly $900 million debt to foreign commercial creditors.
It reached an agreement in principle on the debt last year.
HSBC Markets said in a presentation to the central bank on Monday that Vietnam's sovereign credit rating would probably be Ba3, which indicates a medium level of risk for foreign borrowers.

It said that although there had been a dramatic rise in the country's savings rate -- to 17.5 percent in 1996 from 13.2 percent in 1991 -- there had been a worrying rise in the current account deficit to 11.6 percent of gross domestic product.
